title: Sparse Compact Pool Architecture and Dynamic Scrubber
body:
Summary:
This doc proposes a hybrid KV cache layout and background scrubbing/compaction subsystem designed to reduce long-lived fragmentation on serving hosts while preserving low tail latency for inference. The goal is to: reduce memory overhead from internal fragmentation, bound worst-case allocation latency for hot requests, and provide an operationally simple rollout path that cooperates with existing batching and prefix/KV caching logic.

Motivating observations (empirical + operational):
- Long-lived sequences (chat sessions) produce many small KV entries that linger; over weeks this produces a high fragmentation tail that increases resident set size (RSS) and triggers OOMs under load spikes.
- Large token contexts generate large slab allocations which are hard to pack when the allocator is naive, leaving small holes that pile up.
- Existing eviction-only strategies (LRU-ish) free space but do not reclaim fragmented holes efficiently; background compaction is required.
- Strict lock-free fast-path allocations are critical for per-request latency; any compaction must avoid blocking the hot allocation path.

Design goals (requirements):
1) Fast allocation/free on hot path: sub-microsecond average for common sizes; avoid acquiring global locks.
2) Bounded worst-case allocation latency: fallback pre-allocated emergency pools for critical requests.
3) Fragmentation detection & mitigation: periodic recompaction to reduce RSS without impacting p99 latency.
4) Incremental, low-overhead background compaction ("scrubber") that can be configured per-host and per-customer (Dedicated/Private).
5) Observability: metrics to measure fragmentation, compaction effectiveness, and allocator churn.
6) Back-compat: compatible with current KV API and model-serving threading model.

Core idea (hybrid sparse-compact pool):
- Use a two-tier pool layout per NUMA node: a lightweight fast-path slab allocator for common fixed-size buckets (power-of-two up to a configurable threshold), and a sparse compact arena for variable-size or large entries.
- Slab buckets: keep small and medium fixed-size buckets to serve the hot path with lock-free freelists (per-thread or per-core caches). Buckets should be sized based on telemetry (common 32B, 128B, 1KB, etc).
- Sparse compact arena: for sizes above slab threshold or for internal fragmentation remediation, use a compacting arena built on a sparse occupancy bitmap + small-chunk compaction mover. The arena stores multiple entries packed tightly and keeps an indirection table (compact index) mapping KV handles to packed offsets.
- Indirection table (compact index) is the key to non-blocking compaction: handles presented to runtime are stable (handle -> index entry). During compaction the index is atomically updated to point to the new packed location. Readers see either old or new index atomically; we rely on epoch-based reclamation to retire old memory.

Allocation workflow (hot path):
1) Request size S arrives. If S <= slab_threshold, try per-thread slab fast-path (no global lock). If free chunk found, return handle.
2) If slab fast-path misses, attempt to refill from per-NUMA bucket under a short lock. If still empty, fall back to sparse arena allocation (fast-path path tries a pre-reserved vector of free sparse slots to avoid global slow path).
3) For sparse arena allocation, allocate a compact index slot and place the new payload in a buffer page. Use atomic operations to publish the index mapping.
4) If allocation would exceed resident memory budget, trigger an eviction policy (see below) synchronously for this allocation attempt; if eviction insufficient and this is a critical request, use emergency pre-reserved emergency pool.

Eviction policy (multi-heuristic and workload-aware):
- Primary eviction score = decay-weighted recent access frequency (hotness) combined with size and estimated cost-to-recompute. Use exponentially-weighted moving average for access counts per handle.
- Penalize very large entries for eviction preference (evicting one large entry may free more compactable space).
- Support pinning: some entries (pinned by ongoing requests or explicitly pinned by API) are excluded from eviction.
- Eviction can be incremental and cooperative: background scrubber can opportunistically evict low-score entries to create contiguous regions for compaction.

Background scrubbing & compaction (dynamic scrubber):
- The scrubber runs at a configurable throttle and works per-arena/NUMA node. It performs three activities: (A) identify fragmentation hotspots, (B) move live entries into contiguous ranges, (C) reclaim freed pages or merge into slab refill pools.
- Hotspot detection: track free-run-length distribution and fragmentation ratio (wasted_bytes / total_bytes). When fragmentation > high-water-mark for an arena, schedule compaction tasks.
- Compaction unit: operate on small windows (e.g., 4–64 pages) to bound pause times. Each compaction task creates new destination pages, copies live entries, updates compact index atomically, and then frees old pages under epoch barrier.
- Reader friendliness: compaction uses double-mapping of pages (or copy-on-write) depending on OS support. For non-copyable environments, index swap with epoch reclamation ensures readers either see old or new location without pointer chasing.
- Rate limiting: compactor obeys CPU and memory rate limits, and backoffs when host CPU or latency SLO is under pressure.

Fragmentation tracking & metrics: expose the following observability signals per arena and host:
- fragmentation_ratio = wasted_bytes / total_bytes (time-series).
- free_run_length_histogram (for identifying holes distribution).
- compaction_bytes_moved, compaction_tasks_count, compaction_time_ms_p50/p90/p99.
- allocation_success_fastpath_rate, fastpath_miss_rate, emergency_pool_usage.
- eviction_count, eviction_bytes_freed, eviction_false_positive_rate (evicted then re-requested within window).
- samples of handle lifespan and average object size (for tuning slab buckets).
These metrics allow automated tuning in Redwood Optimize and alerting in Console.

Memory accounting and safety nets:
- Two budgets per arena: soft (target) and hard. Soft budget triggers background compaction + incremental eviction. Hard budget triggers synchronous eviction and eventual request rejections or emergency pool usage.
- Emergency pool: a small pre-committed reserve (tunable per deployment) that services critical requests when main allocator cannot satisfy them. Using it sets a metric flag and will trigger on-call alert if used frequently.

Compatibility & rollout notes:
- The indirection index is backwards-compatible: existing handles map to indices; we maintain a thin compatibility wrapper so current serving code needs minimal change (resolve_handle -> read index -> copy KV).
- Start with disabled (opt-in) compaction in Dedicated/private, with metrics-only mode for Hosted for a period. After collecting fragmentation telemetry and adjusting slab buckets, enable scrubber at low throttle and ramp.
- Provide an admin tool to extract per-arena free-run histograms and to force compaction windows for debugging.

Open questions and tradeoffs (TODOs):
- Index size vs compaction granularity: a compact index entry for every KV introduces overhead; we need simulation to find break-even point where compacting becomes net-win. TODO: run simulator for realistic session traces and report.
- Atomic swap strategy: using 64-bit index CAS works for single-machine but distributed/replicated caches (mirrors) may need coordination. How to handle cross-host migration of pinned entries?
- Page copying cost: for very large tensors, copying during compaction is expensive. Option: avoid copying large objects and rely on large-object eviction heuristics instead. Need ops to annotate objects as "compaction-eligible".
- GC pressure: background copying may increase CPU and transient memory usage. Need tuning knobs and adaptive throttle based on observed p99 latency.

Microbench experiments to run (next steps):
1) Allocation latency microbench with slab thresholds at 512B and 2KB; measure p50/p95/p99 and fastpath hit rate under mixed workloads.
2) Fragmentation simulation: run week-long session trace replay and measure RSS with/without scrubber at different throttles.
3) Compaction window sizing: measure impact on p99 tail for different page-window sizes (4/16/64 pages).
4) Eviction policy ablations: compare LRU vs size-aware decay-weighted policy on throughput and quality of eviction decisions.

Operational playbook (initial):
- Start in metrics-only mode for Hosted for 2 weeks. Tune slab sizes according to the observed object-size histogram.
- Enable scrubber at 5% CPU throttle on Dedicated test cluster for 24–48 hours and monitor fragmentation_ratio, compaction_time_ms_p99, and p99 generation latency.
- If emergency_pool_usage > 0 for > 5 minutes, roll back and investigate root cause.

Appendix: sketches of key data structures (informal):
- SlabBucket { size_class, per_thread_cache[], refill_lock, global_free_list }
- CompactArena { pages[], free_bitmap[], compact_index[], free_run_histogram }
- CompactIndexEntry { atomic_offset, generation, flags } // small, 16B-ish
- ScrubberTask { arena_id, start_page, end_page, target_bytes_to_move, throttle_token }

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc focuses on host-local memory fragmentation; we intentionally do not cover persistent on-disk swap or cross-host shared caches in this iteration.
- Looking for feedback on the indirection table encoding (size vs semantics), and whether a hybrid reference counting + epochs model for reclaim is more robust than pure epoch-based reclamation in our threading model.
- Also want ops input on acceptable emergency_pool sizing heuristics per customer SLA.

Changelog:
- 2025-07-11: initial draft by Riley Chen.
- 2025-08-22: added eviction scoring and observability section (Priya).
- 2025-10-02: clarified compaction windowing and added operational playbook (Miguel, Zoe).

Unresolved action items:
- Simulate traces to choose slab size buckets (owner: Priya).
- Implement prototype compact index and run microbench (owner: Miguel).
- Add Console dashboards for fragmentation metrics (owner: Zoe).

End of doc.
